main.title: F-Zero
main.summary: F-Zero is a 1990 racing game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.text: F-Zero is a 1990 racing game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It was released in Japan on November 21, 1990, in North America in August 1991, and in Europe in 1992. F-Zero is the first game in the F-Zero series and was a launch game for the SNES. F-Zero has been rereleased for the Virtual Console and Nintendo Classics services on various Nintendo platforms, and as part of the Super NES Classic Edition in 2017.

F-Zero takes place in 2560, when multi-billionaires have created a new entertainment based on Formula One races called "F-Zero". The player can choose between one of four characters, each with their own hovercar. The player can race against computer-controlled characters in 15 tracks divided into three leagues.

F-Zero has been acknowledged by critics for setting the standard for the racing genre and the creation of its futuristic subgenre. Critics lauded F-Zero for its fast and challenging gameplay, variety of tracks, and extensive use of the Mode 7 graphics mode. This graphics-rendering technique was an innovative technological achievement at the time that made racing games more realistic. It is credited for reinvigorating the genre and inspiring the future creation of numerous racing games. A sequel, F-Zero X, was released in 1998 for the Nintendo 64.

main.title: Super Mario World
main.summary: Super Mario World is a 1990 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.text: Super Mario World is a 1990 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It was released in Japan in 1990, in North America in 1991 and PAL territories in 1992. The player controls Mario on his quest to save Princess Peach and Dinosaur Land from the series' antagonist Bowser and the Koopalings. The gameplay is similar to that of earlier Super Mario games; players control Mario through a series of levels in which the goal is to reach the goalpost at the end. Super Mario World introduces Yoshi, a rideable dinosaur who can eat enemies and spit some of them out as projectiles.

Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development developed the game, led by director Takashi Tezuka and producer and series creator Shigeru Miyamoto. It is the first Mario game for the SNES and was designed to make the most of the console's technical features. The development team had more freedom compared to the series installments for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). Yoshi was conceptualised during the development of the NES games, but was not used until Super Mario World due to hardware limitations.

Super Mario World is often considered one of the best games in the series and is cited as one of the greatest video games ever made. It sold more than twenty million copies worldwide, making it the best-selling SNES game. It also led to an animated television series and a 1995 prequel, Yoshi's Island. The game has been re-released on multiple occasions: it was part of the 1994 compilation Super Mario All-Stars + Super Mario World for the SNES and was re-released for the Game Boy Advance as Super Mario World: Super Mario Advance 2 in 2001, on the Virtual Console for the Wii, Wii U, and New Nintendo 3DS consoles, and as part of the Super NES Classic Edition. Both the SNES and GBA versions were rereleased for Nintendo Switch as part of the Nintendo Classics service.

main.title: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons
main.subtitle: Smooth scrolling brings platform games to the PC
main.summary: On December 14, 1990, Apogee distributed the first episode of Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons for MS-DOS through bulletin board systems.

cards.heading: Smooth scrolling brings platform games to the PC
cards.text: Apogee distributed the first episode of Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons for MS-DOS on December 14, 1990. The platform game came from the team that would soon found id Software. John Carmack's scrolling technique supported Tom Hall's levels, secrets and young space-travelling hero. The first episode circulated as shareware, with the other two available to buy.

cards.heading: Smooth scrolling changes what the PC can imitate
cards.text: Carmack's technique moved the image by updating only the necessary screen areas, reducing the work needed for smooth side-scrolling on DOS PCs. This gave the team room to build continuous routes of jumps, platforms and secrets. The graphical solution became useful through the movement and spaces designed around it.

cards.heading: Billy Blaze turns the platformer into a child's adventure
cards.text: Billy Blaze is a child genius who builds a spaceship from household objects and leaves for space while his parents are unaware. His pogo stick changes jump height and movement, helping players reach optional routes and hidden rooms. Messages, secrets and unusual aliens give the levels the character of a child's science-fiction adventure.

cards.heading: Shareware means turning the file into distribution
cards.text: Scott Miller's shareware model let the first episode circulate through bulletin board systems from December 14, 1990. Players could try a substantial part of the game before paying for the remaining episodes. The small team reached customers without relying on a retail network, and the first royalties helped convince its members to leave Softdisk. They formally established id Software a few weeks later.

main.title: ActRaiser
main.subtitle: Quintet · Super Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: ActRaiser is Quintet's Super Nintendo game combining side-scrolling action with the development of human settlements. As the Master, the player descends into dangerous regions through an animated warrior statue, then guides the people who begin living there. An angel protects the growing community from above. The two perspectives give victory a consequence that can be watched: after the monsters are defeated, roads and houses appear where the action has made settlement possible. The next journey begins with seeing what those people still need.

cards.heading: First fight, then help a world grow
cards.text: ActRaiser is Quintet's Super Nintendo game combining side-scrolling action with the development of human settlements. As the Master, the player descends into dangerous regions through an animated warrior statue, then guides the people who begin living there. An angel protects the growing community from above. The two perspectives give victory a consequence that can be watched: after the monsters are defeated, roads and houses appear where the action has made settlement possible. The next journey begins with seeing what those people still need.

cards.heading: Miracles have practical uses
cards.text: During the overhead sections, the player directs construction and uses miracles such as rain, sunlight and lightning to make the land habitable. The angel shoots at monsters threatening the population, while expanding settlements eventually seal the lairs producing them. More inhabitants increase the Master's strength, linking the quiet work of planning to survival in the action stages. The player has to understand the region before choosing the right intervention. A field, an obstructed route and a dangerous nest each call for a different kind of help.

cards.heading: A new console finds a musical voice
cards.text: Each region includes action sequences in which the warrior crosses platforms, attacks monsters and confronts a boss. Those encounters bracket the slower development of the community, giving the campaign a rhythm between direct struggle and watching its results. Yuzo Koshiro's score uses the Super Nintendo's sound capabilities for an orchestral character that helped distinguish this early release. Published by Enix in Japan in 1990, ActRaiser made its unusual combination coherent by giving both halves the same purpose: recover a place and make life there possible.

main.title: Kabuki: Quantum Fighter
main.subtitle: Human Entertainment · Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Kabuki: Quantum Fighter is Human Entertainment's NES action platformer about an agent entering a threatened computer system. In the overseas story, Scott O'Connor transfers his consciousness into the machine and takes the appearance of a kabuki performer from his ancestry. His long hair becomes a weapon against the hostile creatures encountered inside. The unusual body gives an otherwise technological mission a memorable physical gesture. Attacking means snapping that hair forward, while the surrounding stages turn the infected machine into a dangerous world of platforms and biological-looking hazards.

cards.heading: A computer mission with a theatrical face
cards.text: Kabuki: Quantum Fighter is Human Entertainment's NES action platformer about an agent entering a threatened computer system. In the overseas story, Scott O'Connor transfers his consciousness into the machine and takes the appearance of a kabuki performer from his ancestry. His long hair becomes a weapon against the hostile creatures encountered inside. The unusual body gives an otherwise technological mission a memorable physical gesture. Attacking means snapping that hair forward, while the surrounding stages turn the infected machine into a dangerous world of platforms and biological-looking hazards.

cards.heading: Swing through the infected machinery
cards.text: Scott runs and jumps through side-scrolling stages, using his hair at close range and chip-based weapons against more distant targets. New weapons broaden the choices available as the mission continues toward each boss. The character's movements make the hardware-inspired scenery feel like a place that can be climbed and crossed. The player has to judge where an attack reaches while keeping the next landing in mind. The visual contrast between theatrical appearance and electronic surroundings remains visible in almost every encounter.

cards.heading: A different story across regions
cards.text: The Japanese release, Jigoku Gokurakumaru, was connected to Kaizo Hayashi's film Zipang and used a different protagonist and narrative background. The overseas edition replaced those references with Scott and the computer emergency while retaining the striking fighter. Released in Japan in late 1990, it reached North America the following year. The adaptation demonstrates how much a story could change around an existing set of actions: the performer remains the centre of the screen even when the explanation for his presence changes.

main.title: Adventures of Lolo 3
main.subtitle: The solution begins before the first step
main.summary: On December 26, 1990, HAL Laboratory released Adventures of Lolo II for Famicom in Japan, the title that would be distributed in the West as Adventures of Lolo 3.

cards.heading: The solution begins before the first step
cards.text: HAL Laboratory released Adventures of Lolo II for the Famicom in Japan on December 26, 1990. Known in the West as Adventures of Lolo 3, it sends Lolo and Lala through Eggerland's puzzle rooms. A field map connects mountains and towers, while boss battles and more action-oriented sections add timing challenges to the familiar blocks, enemies and carefully ordered moves.

cards.heading: The room is a machine to understand before touching it
cards.text: A room's enemies, blocks, hearts and exits create a problem of order. Moving one object can open a route, block an enemy or remove something needed later. Players must consider the resulting positions before committing. Familiar rules become harder to manage as more of them interact within the same enclosed space.

cards.heading: The map turns a sequence of puzzles into a journey
cards.text: The field map links puzzle rooms through mountains and towers. Completing an area returns players to a visible route towards the next challenge. The individual rooms retain their separate solutions, but the map gives their sequence a wider setting and a clearer sense of distance travelled.

cards.heading: When reflex enters the puzzle, the solution must also be executed
cards.text: Some sections require a solution to be carried out at the right moment, with moving enemies and tighter timing. Boss battles add further action to the puzzle structure. Knowing where to go must be combined with occupying the right position as the hazards move. These encounters test execution alongside the plan formed before the first step.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 1991
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 1991/1992 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.

main.title: QuackShot Starring Donald Duck
main.subtitle: A plunger on the trail of treasure
main.summary: In Sega’s 1991 Mega Drive adventure, Donald Duck discovers a map to King Garuzia’s treasure in Scrooge’s library. Huey, Dewey and Louie pilot his plane between destinations, while Pete pursues the same prize. The world map offers choices, but clues and equipment connect the locations into a treasure hunt rather than a simple line of stages.

cards.heading: A plunger on the trail of treasure
cards.text: In Sega’s 1991 Mega Drive adventure, Donald Duck discovers a map to King Garuzia’s treasure in Scrooge’s library. Huey, Dewey and Louie pilot his plane between destinations, while Pete pursues the same prize. The world map offers choices, but clues and equipment connect the locations into a treasure hunt rather than a simple line of stages.

cards.heading: Returning with the right tool
cards.text: Donald’s ordinary plungers temporarily stun enemies. Later versions let him climb walls or hang from flying creatures, changing what he can reach when he returns to a place. Popcorn and bubblegum provide other tools, while checkpoint flags let him call the plane and revisit earlier discoveries. The original Sega instruction booklet makes this back-and-forth structure explicit: an obstacle in one country may require an item found elsewhere. Donald’s expressive animation keeps the adventure recognizably comic, even when the next step demands thought.

main.title: Metroid II: Return of Samus
main.summary: Metroid II: Return of Samus is a 1991 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy.

cards.heading: The mission beneath SR388
cards.text: Metroid II: Return of Samus is a 1991 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy. The first Metroid game for a handheld game console, it was released in North America in November 1991 and in Japan and Europe in 1992. It follows the bounty hunter Samus Aran on her mission to eradicate the Metroids from their home planet, SR388, before the Space Pirates can obtain them. Players must find and exterminate the Metroids to progress.

cards.heading: New ways to move
cards.text: Like the original Metroid, released in 1986 for the Nintendo Entertainment System, Metroid II was developed by Nintendo Research & Development 1 and produced by Gunpei Yokoi. It introduced several features that became staples of the series, including Samus's Space Jump, Spazer Beam and the Spider Ball, and round-shouldered Varia Suit.

cards.heading: Reception and a lasting handheld chapter
cards.text: Metroid II received positive reviews, with praise for its story, setting, and improved gameplay, but was criticized for its graphics and audio. By late 2003, it had sold 1.72 million copies worldwide. It was rereleased on the Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console service in 2011 and on the Nintendo Classics service in February 2023.

cards.heading: Sequels and reinterpretations
cards.text: A sequel, Super Metroid, was released for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System in 1994, and a remake, Metroid: Samus Returns, was released for the Nintendo 3DS in 2017. An unofficial remake, AM2R, was released in 2016 for Windows.

main.title: Civilization
main.summary: Sid Meier's Civilization is a 1991 turn-based strategy 4X video game developed and published by MicroProse.

cards.heading: Civilization
cards.text: Sid Meier's Civilization is a 1991 turn-based strategy 4X video game developed and published by MicroProse. The game was originally developed for MS-DOS running on a PC, and it has undergone numerous revisions for various platforms. The player is tasked with leading an entire human civilization over the course of several millennia by controlling various areas such as urban development, exploration, government, trade, research, and military. The player can control individual units and advance the exploration, conquest and settlement of the game's world. The player can also make such decisions as setting forms of government, tax rates and research priorities. The player's civilization is in competition with other computer-controlled civilizations, with which the player can enter diplomatic relationships that can either end in alliances or lead to war.

cards.heading: Meier, Shelley and the 4X legacy
cards.text: Civilization was designed by Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley following the successes of Silent Service, Sid Meier's Pirates! and Railroad Tycoon. Civilization has sold 1.5 million copies since its release and is considered one of the most influential computer games in history due to its establishment of the 4X genre. In addition to its commercial and critical success, the game has been deemed pedagogically valuable due to its presentation of historical relationships, and one of the greatest video games ever made by several publications. A multiplayer remake, Sid Meier's CivNet, was released for the PC in 1995. Civilization was followed by several sequels starting with Civilization II, with similar or modified scenarios.
